stops.name: The underworld, Aeneas meets her silent shade
stops.campa: In the Fields of Mourning, where those whom cruel love wasted keep to their myrtle groves, Aeneas comes upon her shade, the wound still fresh at her breast. He weeps and pleads that he did not know his leaving would cost her so dear, that he sailed against his own will, by the gods' command. She will not look at him. She keeps her eyes fixed on the ground, no more moved than flint or standing rock, and turns at last into the shadowed wood to Sychaeus, her first husband, who alone answers what is left of her love.
stops.quote: Illa solo fixos oculos aversa tenebat / nec magis incepto vultum sermone movetur / quam si dura silex aut stet Marpesia cautes.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 6.469-471 (Dido's shade turns away in silence)

stops.name: The Numicius, her ghost's last errand, warning her sister
stops.campa: The canon does not let her rest entirely silent. Her sister Anna, fled from Pygmalion's own renewed persecution years later, is shipwrecked near Aeneas's new city in Latium and given shelter, until Lavinia's jealousy threatens her life. In a dream it is Elissa's own shade that comes a last time to warn Anna to flee by night along the river; Anna obeys, is swept into the flood, and rises a nymph of the stream the Romans will call Anna Perenna, the Ides of March forever after held as her festival, her sister's warning the last act love performs.

stops.name: Carthage, Iarbas demands the queen or war
stops.campa: In the older and, the historians insist, the truer telling, the one that grants her no Trojan lover, Iarbas, refused once too often, summons ten of Carthage's chief men and demands the queen in marriage, threatening war. The deputies, afraid to carry it to her face, practice a Punic honesty: the king, they say, asks only for someone to teach his Africans a gentler way of living, and who would leave kin to dwell among barbarians? She reproaches them that no life is too hard for the country's sake, to which life itself is owed; and they spring her own sentence back on her.
stops.quote: She herself, if she wished her city to be secure, must do what she required of others.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.6 (trans. J. S. Watson; the deputies turning the queen's own maxim against her)

stops.name: Carthage, the pyre built as a rite to Sychaeus
stops.campa: She asks three months to prepare herself, and her people, thinking her reconciled to the marriage, grant it gladly. She spends the time not in a bride's dressing but in raising a great pyre at the edge of the city, telling the court it is a sacrifice to release her from her vow to Acerbas before she takes a second husband. Victims are offered; the crowd gathers to watch a wedding-rite, not knowing it is a funeral she has built with her own hands, the last and greatest of the deceptions this Tyrian queen has practiced on a kingdom.

stops.name: Carthage, 'she would go to her husband,' and the sword
stops.campa: She climbs the pyre before the whole city, looks out over the people she led out of Tyre and built a nation for, and tells them plainly that she goes now to her husband, as they themselves desired of her: meaning Sychaeus, not Iarbas, and every listener understands the true meaning only as the blade goes in. She dies by her own hand rather than break a vow twenty years kept, and Carthage, unable to punish or undo it, does what the ancient world always does with a woman it cannot control: it makes her a goddess and worships her as long as the city stands.
stops.quote: She would go to her husband, as they had desired her.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.6 (trans. J. S. Watson)

stops.name: Byrsa, the avenger from her bones is born: Hannibal
stops.campa: Six hundred years after the pyre, in a city still climbing the same Byrsa hill, still marked by the sign of Tanit and the memory of a queen who would not be owned, a son is born to Hamilcar Barca and named Hannibal. The poets' curse, let an avenger rise out of my bones to hunt them with fire and iron, finds, whether cause or coincidence the histories will never quite settle, a bearer at last; within a generation this child will bring war to Italy's own gates in a way no Tyrian exile's sword ever could.
stops.quote: Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 4.625 (Dido's curse, read by later Rome as prophecy of Hannibal)

stops.name: Carthage burns, the curse's furthest reach
stops.campa: The Third Punic War ends where Elissa's city began: Scipio Aemilianus takes Byrsa street by street, burns what six centuries built on an ox-hide's measure of ground, and is said to weep even as he watches, quoting Homer on the fall of sacred Troy and foreseeing, in the ashes of the queen's own city, a day when Rome itself might burn the same way. The sign of Tanit goes dark on its last stelae. Whatever the historians make of the coincidence, the curse and the city that carried it end, by Roman hands, within the same generation of each other's memory.

stops.name: Colonia Julia Carthago, Rome refounds the queen's city
stops.campa: A century after the burning, the line that Elissa's own curse was said to have cost so dearly returns to raise her city again: Julius Caesar plans a Roman colony on the ruined Byrsa, and Augustus, his heir, completes it as Colonia Iulia Carthago, capital once more of Roman Africa. The queen who measured out a kingdom in ox-hide strips, cursed the ancestor of her refounder, and burned rather than be owned, gives her name and her hill to the empire her own poets had made her enemy, the last and strangest turn in a story the ancient world never tired of retelling.
